title: Quantum Key Distribution Without Shared Reference Frame Under Unital Noise
authors: Junaid ur Rehman, Shehbaz Tariq, Symeon Chatzinotas
abstract: We consider a general and practical scenario of quantum key distribution (QKD) over an unknown, stationary, unital qubit channel. Furthermore, due to practical limitations, e.g., relative movement and rotation of communicating parties, a global shared reference frame cannot be established. This scenario can routinely appear in satellite QKD. We propose two methods to overcome the physical qubit noise and the lack of shared reference frame. The first proposed approach involves constructing the Pauli transfer matrix (PTM) description of the channel, which we achieve without requiring a shared reference frame, by absorbing the lack of shared reference frame in the channel definition. This is followed by the identification of singular vectors of PTM as the Bloch vectors for optimal signal states. In the optimized local bases, the resulting correlations are equivalent, up to outcome relabeling, to those of a Pauli channel, allowing us to show the optimality of the BB84 and six-state QKD protocols under these conditions. The second approach, called the sequential basis matching (SBM) involves sequentially identifying the channel-optimized local bases that enable QKD. We show that both of these approaches result in the same effective key exchange rate for QKD.
summary: This paper tackles the practical challenge of Quantum Key Distribution when communicating parties lack a shared reference frame over noisy channels. The authors introduce two robust methods—PTM analysis and Sequential Basis Matching—to determine optimal local measurement bases. They prove these methods yield equivalent, enhanced key rates compared to standard protocols, significantly improving theoretical performance estimates for real-world quantum links.
main_problem: The core problem is establishing secret keys via Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) when communication occurs over an unknown, stationary, unital qubit channel without the communicating parties sharing a global reference frame.
main_result: Both proposed methods—Pauli Transfer Matrix (PTM) analysis and Sequential Basis Matching (SBM)—yield equivalent results, demonstrating that optimized local signaling can recover positive key rates even when standard assumptions about basis alignment fail.
method: The authors propose two complementary theoretical approaches: one using the PTM derived from channel characterization via SVD, and another operational approach called SBM that iteratively optimizes measurement bases based on observed error probabilities.
model_or_system: The system models QKD over a qubit channel characterized by unknown unitaries ($U_A, U_B$) and unital noise ($\mathcal{N}$). The analysis relies heavily on the Pauli basis representation of quantum states and channels.
key_observables: Secret key rates (for BB84 and six-state protocols), Quantum Bit Error Rates (QBERs) in X, Y, and Z bases, and the effective channel's PTM parameters.
important_parameters: The channel noise strength ($\epsilon$), which quantifies the deviation from ideal transmission; the number of measurement shots ($N_s$) for finite-sample analysis.
main_assumptions: The quantum channel is assumed to be stationary and unital. The primary challenge addressed is the violation of the shared reference frame assumption, rather than modeling specific physical noise sources like loss or dark counts.
figures_summary: Figures compare secret key rates vs. channel parameter $\epsilon$ for standard versus optimized signaling; they also show QBER sets and finite-sample estimations demonstrating convergence to the theoretical PTM rate.
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the physical challenge (QKD without shared reference frame). It then details two mathematical approaches: 1) Constructing the effective channel via PTM/SVD, and 2) Implementing SBM for sequential basis optimization. Finally, it compares the results and analyzes performance robustness.
why_interesting: This work is highly relevant to quantum optics and open quantum systems because it provides a rigorous framework for optimizing communication protocols under realistic, non-ideal environmental constraints (like relative motion in satellite links) that violate idealized assumptions of perfect alignment.

figures.caption: Fig. 1. The system model. The transmitter and receiver lack a shared reference frame, which is exemplified as a satellite-to-ground quantum communication link where the local frames of reference do not coincide with the global reference. Polarization encoding of photons in global reference frame does not translate to the same in either of the local references.

Fig. 2. Secret key rate (bits per sifted detected signal) as a function of channel parameter ϵ. The optimized signaling, as proposed in the main text, compensates well for the absence of shared reference frame, as evidenced by the ideal secret key rate for the unitary/noiseless channel up to an unknown rotation, i.e., ϵ = 1.

Fig. 3. Secret key rate (bits per sifted detected signal) as a function of QBERs in Z and X basis. The scatter points show the QBERs of numerical simulations with (a) standard, i.e., without basis optimization, and (b) optimized basis BB84 in random unitary channels.

Fig. 4. Robustness checks for the optimized signaling. (a) Positive-key probability, Pr{R > 0}, over the random unitary channel ensemble as a function of the channel parameter ϵ. (b) Finite-sample PTM-based basis estimation for BB84 at ϵ = 0.8, shown as a function of the number of shots per PTM entry, Ns. (c) Corresponding finite-sample PTM-based basis estimation for six-state QKD at ϵ = 0.8. In (b) and (c), the dashed line denotes the exact-PTM asymptotic rate, the finite-sample curve denotes the rate computed from the noisy estimated PTM, and the achieved-rate curve denotes the rate obtained when the finite-sample optimized bases are applied to the underlying simulated channel.
